sentences.text: Allosaurus was a large bipedal predator with a light, robust skull equipped with dozens of sharp, serrated teeth. Its anatomy featured small three-fingered hands relative to its powerful legs and a long, muscular tail that balanced its body.

While the average specimen of A. fragilis measured between 7.5 and 8 meters, the largest individuals reached 9 meters. However, skeletal remains from the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry show a wide size range, from less than 1 meter to 12 meters in length.

Allosaurus was discovered during the 'Bone Wars', a rivalry between Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope that spurred fossil discoveries in the Western US. The first fossil described in its history was a bone obtained by Ferdinand V. Hayden in 1869. The first definitive remains were described in 1877 by Othniel C. Marsh, who named the species Allosaurus fragilis that same year.

As an apex predator in the Morrison Formation, Allosaurus likely preyed on large herbivorous dinosaurs including ornithopods, stegosaurids, and sauropods. Histological analysis suggests the animal stopped growing at around 22 to 28 years of age, similar to other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus. A juvenile specimen reveals that young individuals had relatively longer legs, with the shin and foot segments longer than the thigh.
The famous 'Big Al' specimen was a subadult estimated to be only 87% grown, making it smaller than the average adult Allosaurus.
Allosaurus is classified in the family Allosauridae. The genus was established by Marsh in 1877, with A. fragilis designated as the type species.
Proposed species include A. europaeus, A. jimmadseni, and A. anax. The classification has been complicated by the extreme fragmentary nature of the type specimen of A. fragilis (YPM 1930).

Allosaurus fossils date to the Late Jurassic period, specifically living during the late Upper Jurassic between 155 and 145 million years ago, spanning the Oxfordian to Titonian stages. Fossils have been found in what is now North America and Europe.

Statistical analyses by David K. Smith between 1996 and 1999 suggested that morphological differences in Morrison Formation Allosaurus specimens represent individual variation rather than distinct species. The validity of A. europaeus has been debated, with studies arguing it is a synonym of A. fragilis, a nomen dubium, or requires re-evaluation. In 2024, André Burigo and Mateus identified nine unique features in the Vale Frades specimen that support the validity of A. europaeus.
